excerpt: What a security analyst actually does in a shift, the three questions behind every alert, and the path in for somebody starting from a non-technical job.

body.text: This lesson describes the work of a cybersecurity analyst: what fills the shift, what the alerts mean, and how somebody without a computer degree gets in. You will see the job as it is, rather than as a film about hackers.
An analyst watches a company's systems for signs of trouble, decides what matters, and writes down what happened. Most of the work is reading, judging, and writing, with the tools doing the watching.
Before you start

items: About twenty minutes of reading.
Any experience you already have with troubleshooting, which counts.
A notebook, if you want to write down the terms.

body.text: A shift, in order

items: Read the handover notes from the previous shift, which say what is still open.
Open the alert queue and start from the oldest or the most severe.
For each alert, check the account, the device, and the time.
Decide whether it is a real problem or expected activity.
Close the false ones with a note, and escalate the real ones.
Write the end-of-shift notes, so the next person starts where you stopped.

body.text: You will see a screen with a list of alerts ranked by severity, each with a time stamp, a rule name, and a device or account. Clicking one opens the details, which is where the judgement begins.

body.alt: A security monitor showing a grid of alerts and system status panels.
body.caption: The queue is the day's work. Most items are noise, and the skill is telling the few real ones from the many expected ones.

body.text: It looks like the job is spotting clever attacks. Most of it is answering the same three questions quickly, and doing that hundreds of times without losing accuracy.
The three questions

items: Is this normal for this account or device, at this hour?
Has it happened before, and what was the outcome then?
If it is real, what is the damage and who must know within the hour?

body.text: A login at two in the morning from a country the company does not operate in is worth a call. The same login at nine in the morning from the office is routine, even though both arrive as the same alert.
What the notes look like
The written record is half the job. A clear note lets the next analyst act without repeating your work.

items: What happened, in one sentence, with the time.
Which account, device, or system was involved.
What you checked, and what you found.
What you decided, and why.
What you did next, and who you told.
What is still open, so the handover is honest.

body.alt: A desk with notes, a keyboard, and a screen showing an incident record.
body.caption: The note is the work. A ticket that the next person can act on is worth more than a clever diagnosis nobody wrote down.

body.text: Skills that matter more than the tools

items: Reading a log line and finding the part that matters.
Asking a colleague for help without wasting an hour.
Writing three clear sentences under time pressure.
Knowing when to wake somebody up, and when to wait until morning.
Patience with repetition, since the queue refills every few minutes.
Curiosity about how a system is supposed to work, so you notice when it does not.

body.text: None of this needs a degree to begin. A certificate covers the vocabulary, and the judgement comes from doing the queue.
Do not worry if the tool names sound unfamiliar. Every employer uses a different set, and each one takes a fortnight to learn.
Getting in from another job

items: Start with the free tier of a security course, and finish it rather than collecting five.
Learn basic networking: addresses, ports, and what a firewall does.
Practise on legal practice sites, which give you a safe place to try.
Look for a support desk role first, which is the usual doorway.
Write a short CV that names the tools you have touched, even in a lab.
Ask at your current workplace whether the security team needs help with anything.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here is a normal part of the job, not a sign that you are unsuited to it.

items: You closed a real alert as false: report it as soon as you notice, which is what the notes are for.
You escalated something harmless: that is cheaper than the opposite, and nobody will mind.
The queue is unmanageable: tell the shift lead, rather than staying silent and skipping items.
You do not understand a tool: read its documentation search, which is faster than guessing.
You feel out of your depth in the first month: most analysts do, and the queue is the teacher.
The handover note is unclear: ask the previous shift, rather than assuming.

body.text: Practice
Do one small piece of the job this week, from home.

items: Read about one alert type, such as a failed login burst.
Find a legal practice site and work through one beginner exercise.
Write a sample ticket in the six lines above, as if you had closed it.
Learn what a port number is, in one paragraph.
Note one tool name you keep hearing and read its front page.

body.text: You now know what the job looks like from the desk. In the next lesson you will see the room where this work happens all night.

excerpt: What a security operations centre looks like, how the tiers divide the work, and how a night shift hands over to a morning team without losing a detail.

body.text: This lesson describes the security operations centre, usually called the SOC: the room, the screens, the tiers of staff, and the handover between shifts. You will see why the room never closes and what each level of analyst actually handles.
A SOC is a team watching one organisation's systems all day and all night. The room is less dramatic than films suggest: several screens, a shared queue, and a great deal of writing.
Before you start

items: About twenty minutes of reading.
The previous lesson on the analyst's work, if you have not read it.

body.text: What is in the room

items: A large screen showing the health of key systems, visible from every desk.
Individual desks with the alert queue and the ticketing system.
A call list of who to wake, in what order, and at which hour.
A whiteboard or a shared page for what is happening right now.
A separate channel for the organisation's own staff to report a problem.
A quiet corner, because a serious incident needs one conversation at a time.

body.text: You will see the same dashboard on several screens, which looks wasteful until you understand that everybody must see the same picture at the same moment.

body.alt: A monitoring room with several screens showing dashboards and alert queues.
body.caption: The wall screen shows the state of the systems. The desks show the work, which is the queue and the tickets.

body.text: It looks like the room exists to watch hackers. It mostly exists to notice a broken backup, a full disk, or a door sensor, which cause more trouble than intruders.
The tiers, in plain words

items: First tier: reads every alert, closes the noise, and escalates what looks real.
Second tier: takes escalations, investigates deeper, and contains the damage.
Third tier: handles the hardest cases, hunts for what the alerts missed, and improves the rules.
The shift lead: decides who works on what, and calls the manager when it is serious.
The incident manager: runs the response, including who speaks to whom.
Engineers: keep the tools working, so the analysts can see what is happening.

body.text: A first-tier analyst might close forty alerts and escalate three in a shift. That ratio is normal, and closing forty correctly is the skill that keeps the team sane.
The night shift

items: Fewer people, and more of the work is waiting and checking.
The queue often looks quiet, which is when a careful analyst looks at what the day shift had no time for.
Escalation rules change at night: the threshold for waking somebody is higher and clearer.
The handover note matters more, because nobody senior is in the room.
Health matters: eat properly, take the break, and do not drive home tired.
The morning team reads your notes before they speak to you, so write them well.

body.alt: A dimly lit operations room at night with one analyst at a desk.
body.caption: The night shift is quieter and heavier. The notes carry the whole story into the morning.

body.text: The handover
A good handover takes ten minutes and prevents a duplicated investigation or a dropped one.

items: Read the previous notes before the shift starts, not after the first alert.
List the open tickets with the next step for each.
Name the systems already known to be unstable, so nobody mistakes them for an attack.
Say what you would look at first, if you were staying.
Ask questions while the outgoing person is still there.
Sign the handover, which makes the record clear about who knew what.

body.text: None of this needs expensive software. A shared page with three headings, open, watching, and closed, does the work in a small team.
Do not worry about asking a question during handover that sounds basic. A question at handover is cheaper than a mistake at three in the morning.
If it goes wrong
Every case here happens in real rooms, and each has a routine answer.

items: An alert is missed on a quiet night: the process, not one person, is reviewed and the rule is fixed.
Two analysts investigate the same thing: the shared queue exists to prevent this, so use it.
The wall screen fails: the work continues on the desks, since the queue is the source.
Nobody knows who to call: the call list is out of date. Update it during the day.
The night is too quiet to stay awake: use the time for reading the rules, not for scrolling.
The morning shift disagrees with your decision: write down the reason, which settles most disputes.

body.text: Practice
Write a handover note as an exercise.

items: Imagine three open tickets: one false alarm, one watching, one real.
Write six lines about each, as if handing over.
Name the first thing the next person should check.
Mark which one should wake somebody, and why.
Read it aloud and remove anything vague.

body.text: You can now picture the room where this work happens. In the next lesson you will understand the system that fills the screens with alerts.

excerpt: What a SIEM collects, how a rule turns log lines into an alert, why the same alert fires all day, and how tuning cuts the noise.

body.text: This lesson explains a SIEM in ordinary words: what it collects, how it decides something is worth an alert, and why the same alert fires all day. You will learn the three parts and the tuning that makes the numbers useful.
SIEM stands for security information and event management. The name describes two jobs: collecting records from many systems, and managing the alerts that come out of them.
Before you start

items: About twenty minutes.
The earlier lessons on the analyst and the room, if you want the sequence.

body.text: Three parts, in order

items: Collection: the SIEM pulls log lines from servers, firewalls, laptops, and cloud accounts.
Storage: it keeps them for a set period, often ninety days or a year, because investigations look backwards.
Rules: it checks each incoming line against conditions that somebody wrote.
Alerts: when a rule matches, the system raises a ticket for a person to read.
Dashboards: charts showing counts over time, which reveal a change rather than a single event.
Reports: a summary written for managers, often monthly, on what was seen and fixed.

body.text: You will see a single log line look unremarkable: a time, an account name, an action, and a source address. Ten thousand of those lines together show a pattern, which is what the SIEM is for.

body.alt: A screen of log lines with timestamps, user names, and addresses.
body.caption: One line says little. The value comes from thousands of lines kept in order, searchable by account, device, and time.

body.text: It looks like the SIEM finds attacks by intelligence. It finds them by comparing records against rules people wrote, and by showing what changed from yesterday.
How a rule becomes an alert

items: A rule might say: five failed logins for one account within ten minutes.
Another might say: a login from a country no employee has visited.
Another: a large download from a finance folder outside working hours.
The rule matches a pattern across lines, not a single line.
The match produces an alert with the evidence attached.
A person then decides whether the pattern means trouble.

body.text: The alert screen will show the rule name, the time, the accounts involved, and a small table of the matching events. That table is the evidence, and reading it takes less time than reading the rule.

body.alt: A dashboard showing alert counts by severity over a week.
body.caption: A chart shows the change. A flat line that jumps on Tuesday morning is the signal, and the alert list explains why.

body.text: Why the same alert fires all day
A rule that fires constantly is usually too broad. This is called a noisy rule, and it teaches the team to ignore the queue, which is dangerous.

items: A scanner runs every morning at six, and every scan raises a rule.
A backup account logs in from the same server nightly.
One application retries a failed password four times by design.
A rule flags every administrator login, which is thousands a day.
A new device sends unexpected traffic until it is registered.
A single rule written for one department fires across the whole company.

body.text: None of these are attacks. Each one is a rule that needs a condition attached, such as ignoring the scanner's address or the backup account.

If you have ever wondered why a security team ignores an alert you found alarming, this is usually the reason. The rule fired for a reason that has nothing to do with an attack, and you are seeing the pattern it produces.
Tuning, in practice

items: Read the alerts a rule produces for a week before changing it.
Find the common reason each one is false, and write it down.
Add an exception for that specific case, not for the whole rule.
Test the change against last month's records, to see what would have been missed.
Ask the system owner to confirm the exception is safe.
Record the change, so the next analyst knows why it exists.

body.text: Do not worry about missing something by tuning. A rule that nobody reads catches nothing, and a narrow rule that everybody reads catches what matters.
When you tune a rule, write down what you changed and why, because you will be the person asking in six months. Your note is what stops the next analyst from undoing your work by accident.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is a known problem with a known correction.

items: No alerts arrive at all: collection has stopped. Check the feed before checking the rules.
Alerts are delayed by hours: the queue is overloaded, or the storage is full.
The same alert repeats in hundreds: the rule is too broad. Add the exception.
A real event produced no alert: the rule does not cover it. Write one, and test it.
The dashboard shows nothing: the time filter is set to a quiet period.
Logs are missing from one system: its agent is down, or the clock is wrong.

body.text: Practice
Write one rule in plain words, then find its weakness.

items: Choose a pattern worth watching, such as failed logins.
Write the rule as one sentence with numbers and a time window.
List three normal situations that would also match it.
Add an exception for each, in words.
Explain the rule to somebody who does not work in security.

body.text: You can now read a dashboard and know what produced it. In the next lesson you will see the principle that changed how networks are built.

excerpt: What never trust, always verify means in practice, the three checks at every door, and why an office network is no longer treated as safe.

body.text: This lesson explains zero trust, the principle that no request is trusted because of where it comes from. You will learn the three checks applied at every door, what least privilege means, and why the old idea of a safe office network failed.
Zero trust means verify every request, every time: who is asking, from what device, and for what. A familiar network is not a reason to stop checking.
Before you start

items: About twenty minutes.
No technical background needed.

body.text: The old model

items: Once you were inside the office network, you could reach most systems.
The boundary was a firewall, and everything inside it was treated as friendly.
A stolen laptop on the office wifi inherited that trust.
A single phishing email could put an attacker inside the wall.
Remote work then moved people outside the wall entirely.
The model assumed the inside was safe, and the inside was not always safe.

body.text: You will see the difference in a login: the old system asked for a password once and then stopped asking. A zero-trust system keeps checking, quietly, in the background.

body.alt: A person passing a checkpoint where an identity card is checked.
body.caption: Every request passes a checkpoint. Being recognised once does not open every door afterwards.

body.text: It looks like zero trust means trusting nobody, which would make work impossible. It means trusting evidence at each step, rather than the location of the request.
The three checks

items: Identity: the person is who they claim, proven by a password plus a second factor.
Device: the laptop or phone is known, patched, and has its screen lock on.
Context: the time, the place, and the request match what this person normally does.
Access is granted for the specific system needed, not for the network as a whole.
The permission expires, so yesterday's access is not today's.
Every action is logged, which makes the checks reviewable afterwards.

body.text: A request that fails any one check is refused or challenged with a second step. A correct password from an unknown device in a new country will trigger another question, which is the system working.
On a phone, you will see a prompt asking you to approve the sign-in, with the time and the city shown underneath. If the city is wrong, refuse it and change the password.

body.alt: A corridor of separate doors each requiring a badge.
body.caption: Each door has its own check. Access to the reception is not access to the records room.

body.text: Least privilege, in daily life
Least privilege means giving each person the smallest access that lets them work. It applies far beyond offices.

items: A shop assistant does not need the owner's bank login.
A temporary staff member gets access for the weeks they work.
A shared account should be a named account, so the log shows a person.
An app asking for full access to your files rarely needs it.
An administrator uses a normal account for email and a separate one for changes.
Access is removed on the day somebody leaves, not at the end of the month.

body.text: None of this slows ordinary work. Most people notice one extra approval on a phone, and nothing else.
Do not worry about the word zero in the name. It describes trust in the network, not trust in people, who are still the reason the systems exist.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is a friction that has an answer, and each is worth the friction.

items: You are asked to verify again: the device or location changed, which is the check doing its job.
A colleague cannot reach a system: their permission expired. Ask for it, rather than sharing yours.
An old device blocks access: it needs an update before it is allowed back.
A vendor needs access: give one system and a date, never the whole network.
The approval process is slow: that is a process problem to raise, not a reason to bypass it.
Somebody shares a password to save time: report it, since it removes every check at once.

body.text: Practice
Apply the idea to your own accounts this week.

items: List the apps that can read your email or files.
Remove access from the two you do not use.
Turn on two-step verification on your main account.
Check which devices are signed in, and sign out the unknown ones.
Give a family member a limited role rather than your own password.

body.text: You can now see why every door has a check. In the next lesson you will look for the weak places before somebody else finds them.

excerpt: How a vulnerability assessment finds weak points, what a severity score means in practice, and the report that gets a problem fixed.

body.text: This lesson explains a vulnerability assessment: a scan for weak places in systems, a decision about which to fix first, and a report that gets somebody to act. You will learn what the scan can see, what it cannot, and how severity scores are read.

A vulnerability assessment checks what is known to be weak, using lists of published problems. It finds missing updates, open services, and default settings, which are the causes of most real incidents.
Before you start

items: About twenty minutes.
The earlier lesson on the analyst's work, for context.

body.text: How the check runs

items: Agree the scope in writing, listing the systems that may be scanned.
Get permission from the owner, since scanning without it is a legal risk.
Run the scan outside working hours, because it can slow older machines.
Read the results and remove duplicates and false matches.
Confirm the serious findings by hand, rather than trusting the tool alone.
Write the report with an owner and a deadline for each finding.

body.text: You will see a results list with each finding naming a system, a port or a service, and a reference number for the published weakness. The reference number is the part you paste into a search when you need the details.

body.alt: A person checking a fence with a torch, looking for gaps.
body.caption: The scan walks the perimeter and reports gaps. It says nothing about whether somebody is already inside.

body.text: It looks like a scan finds attackers. It finds weaknesses, and a weakness is only a risk when somebody uses it, so the report ranks what to fix first.
Reading a severity score

items: The score runs from zero to ten, and the label is usually low, medium, high, or critical.
A score describes the weakness in general, not your system in particular.
A critical weakness on a machine nobody can reach is less urgent than a high one on the internet.
Ask two questions: is it reachable, and does it hold valuable data?
A missing update that a scanner can exploit from outside is the first thing to fix.
A finding on a test machine with no data can wait behind a real one.

body.text: The report will group findings by system and by severity, which is the fastest way to see where the work is. One old server often produces half the list.

body.alt: A printed scan report with severity labels beside each finding.
body.caption: A report with owners and dates gets fixed. A report with only severity labels gets filed.

body.text: The report that gets action
A finding with no owner and no date stays open for years. The report decides whether the work happens.

items: State the risk in business terms: what could be lost, not only the technical name.
Name one owner per finding, by role rather than by team.
Set a date that matches the severity, such as seven days for critical.
Say what the fix is, in one sentence, so nobody has to research it.
Include how the fix will be checked, which closes the loop.
Keep a summary page of counts, since managers read that page first.

body.text: None of this needs a special tool. A spreadsheet with system, finding, owner, date, and status does the work in a small organisation.
Do not worry about the list being long after the first scan. The first one always is, and the second is shorter because the same findings are being fixed.
What a scan cannot do

items: It cannot tell whether a password was written on a note beside the screen.
It cannot find a weakness in a process, such as access nobody removes.
It cannot see a trick that persuades a person to hand over a code.
It cannot prove that a system is safe, only that known problems are missing.
It cannot replace a test where a person tries to break in on purpose.
It cannot fix anything, which is why the report matters more than the scan.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here is common, and each has a routine correction.

items: The scan reports everything as critical: the tool is set too loud. Confirm findings by hand.
The scan slows a server: run it outside working hours, and exclude fragile machines.
Nothing is found at all: the scan could not reach the systems. Check the credentials.
The same findings return every quarter: nobody owns them. Add names and dates.
A system owner refuses the scan: raise it with their manager, since the scope was agreed.
A finding is wrong: record it as a false positive with a reason, which stops it returning.

body.text: Practice
Write a report for a system you know, even a home network.

items: List three systems you own and what each one holds.
Check whether each has its updates installed.
Note the weakest one, and why it is reachable.
Write one line naming an owner and a date.
Fix the simplest finding today, and mark it closed.

body.text: You can now turn a scan into work that gets done. In the next lesson you will see how a message actually travels across a network.
